tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

# Two CLIP Plays: A Failed Block and Clean Protection

**What it is** — Jenkins shows two plays, each with a field map shaded by each lineman's value, a time series every tenth of a second, and a whole-line value (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [04:31], [05:01]).

**Failed block.** A Tua Tagovailoa completion to a receiver (captions: "Tua tangaloa", "mik aeki") where two linemen "fail their assignment" and the quarterback is pressured. Green means above expectation and red below; the model flags the two linemen in red as lowering the chance of a successful play (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [04:01], [04:31]). Values change over time with each lineman's features. The whole-line value starts at 0.10 to 0.15 (captions "01 to 0.15"), read as 10 to 15 percent of the completion attributable to the line, something he says correlation-only metrics "cannot state" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [05:01]).

**Clean protection.** A Jimmy Garoppolo completion to Deebo Samuel (captions "Jimmy Garoppolo", "Debo Samuel") with plenty of space; shading runs purple to green because everyone contributed positively and no pressure was allowed. Best performers named: "Daniel brunskill" (caption spelling); one of the worst, Trent Williams, "but he's still positive". The line total is 0.6 to 0.8 (captions "6 to8"), read as 60 to 80 percent of the play attributable to the line (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [05:31], [06:01]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism for why the line share differs so much between plays (10 to 15 percent versus 60 to 80 percent), and the talk does not explain it. Inference: because the estimand is the effect of allowing pressure, a play with no pressure allowed makes the positive values hard to interpret as that effect, and the speaker does not say how.

**When to apply** — As a worked pair to test understanding of the output: one can read a lineman's value as a play-level, time-varying credit. Inference: a usable film-review exercise is to check the two flagged linemen against film for the assignment failure the speaker describes.

Eric's baseline: Eric's baseline has no football-play method; the closest standing rule is "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q3.)

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: two hand-picked plays, one outcome each, no distribution of values, and no check that the model's read of "who failed" matches film beyond the speaker's statement that it "correctly" identified them (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [04:31]). The 10 to 15 versus 60 to 80 percent line shares are unexplained and the captions for both ranges are garbled, so the exact figures may differ. A single play is not evidence of accuracy.

**Example** — This entry is the example; see the two plays above.

**Related** — [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]]; [[claim--clip-validation-against-honors-salary-and-pff]]; [[principle--player-credit-is-a-causal-question-not-a-prediction-residual]]. Contrast with the pass-rush side example in [[principle--credit-pass-rush-pressure-throughout-the-play]] (SSAC24).

**What it is** — Evan Monroe shows the 2019 season under his rule: the second-last team (captions "the feet Suns") gets the highest probability because many of its losses came late in the season, which did not count toward its odds (-6pe_zOKCig [19:31], [20:02]). # Defensive Three-Point Percentage Looks Like a Coin Flip, Yet Defenders Affect Shots: "Defending the Three Means Avoiding It"

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") says that, in his view, defensive three-point percentage, at team or individual level, "is not really a thing", because what happens once the shot leaves the offensive player's hands is "out of the defense's hands" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:48], [16:18]). Support: a graph by another writer (caption spelling "Hest Becker") indicating that individual defensive three-point percentage "looks a lot like a coin flip would look" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [16:18]). He then qualifies it: he is "not saying that it is just luck", only that it looks like it would if it were (BJkCqf6Fj2w [16:48]). Where defenders do affect a shot:
- Distance: a shooter four feet from the defender on a catch-and-shoot shoots about 34%, at ten feet about 40% (BJkCqf6Fj2w [16:48], [17:18]).
- Fouls: fouling a jump shooter "turns a 35% shot into a 75 or 80% shot" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [17:18]).
- Late shot clock and end-of-game situations show low three-point percentages "even controlling for all other factors", but he says that style of defense is not available in regular play, because a defender must also stop the drive (BJkCqf6Fj2w [17:18], [17:48]).
His conclusion: a catch-and-shoot three below roughly 34% is usually not taken, and "even a 34% three is a 51% effective shot", so "defending the three means avoiding the three entirely" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [17:48], [18:19]). He uses baseball's batting average on balls in play (BABIP) as the analogy, noting that in baseball the "no control" idea was later "relaxed a fair amount" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:18], [15:48]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives a partial mechanism: the contest affects the shot only through distance, fouls and clock context, and most of the defensive effect shows up as shots not taken (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:18], [18:19]). The coin-flip comparison itself is shown with a graph by another writer and no detail.

**When to apply** — As a caution against using an outcome rate the defense does not control as a skill metric, and as an example of the risk of reading a flat distribution as "luck". Inference: the same caution applies to any Baylor metric whose variation looks random at the individual level, where one should ask what the measure does not capture before using it to judge a person. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2a): "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise."

**When NOT to apply** — Contested within the talk itself: he says the percentage is "not really a thing" and looks like a coin flip, and in the same passage lists real defender effects (distance, fouls, late clock). The coin-flip evidence is a single graph from another writer with no detail shown, and the 34% and 40% figures have no sample or source stated aloud. The caption "worth 50% less" at 20 feet at the end of the talk is unclear (BJkCqf6Fj2w [19:50]) and should not be relied on. NBA only; a statement about one metric, not about defensive skill in general.

**Example** — The talk's: a 34% three is a 51% effective shot, so a defense cannot make such shots unattractive except by preventing them (BJkCqf6Fj2w [18:19]).

# Four Drivers of More Threes: Skill, Permission, Downsizing and Catching the Ball Farther Out

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") ends with what he calls "one truth" and then says all of it is "still just a theory" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [18:50], [21:22]). Teams work harder to create threes because a longer jump shot is more valuable than the jump shots already taken. Four factors (BJkCqf6Fj2w [18:50], [19:20], [19:50]):
- **Individual skill development:** players working more on long-distance shooting because the three "is a vital piece to getting playing time" and staying in the league.
- **Permission:** teams encourage and permit players with that skill to step out and shoot.
- **Downsizing:** less time with two traditional big men and more shooters on the floor.
- **Strategy that changes where players catch the ball:** to take a catch-and-shoot three, the ball must be caught outside the arc, so teams changed where players catch it; "worth 50% less" at 20 feet is unclear in the captions (BJkCqf6Fj2w [19:50]).
Evidence for the net effect: perimeter players have long had high three-point rates, but over the last four years power forwards' three-point rate "jumped substantially", most teams play with four shooters and this year more often five (BJkCqf6Fj2w [20:20], [20:51]). His summary: "people are stepping further away from the basket" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [20:51]). In Q&A he adds a limit: there is "probably" a ceiling on how many players have the skill to space the floor (BJkCqf6Fj2w [23:56]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives these as his theory and does not test any one cause. Inference: with four causes named together and no attribution among them, the account cannot say which one mattered most.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when explaining a league-wide strategy shift: ask separately about skill supply, coach permission, roster design and scheme. Inference: Baylor's analogue is any change in practice or testing culture, where individual skill, staff permission, roster mix and process changes may each contribute and should be asked about separately.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the speaker's own theory, with the only data a power-forward rate chart that the captions do not describe. He acknowledges "better theories" may replace his (BJkCqf6Fj2w [21:22]). He declined to answer a question on how teams measure chains of actions and how advanced they are, saying his team's work is private (BJkCqf6Fj2w [22:25], [22:55]). NBA only, through the 2017 All-Star break (BJkCqf6Fj2w [20:20]).

**Example** — From the talk: power forwards' three-point rate "jumped substantially" over four years while perimeter players' rates were already high (BJkCqf6Fj2w [20:20]).

# Modeled Wage Savings: About 11% Less Salary Spent on Predicted Injuries

**What it is** — The presenters translate injuries into money using salary data from Capology: wages "spent" on players who are injured and so unavailable (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [12:46]). Reported: Brighton would have saved the most, a 22% reduction in salary cost tied to predicted injuries, and across all Premier League clubs the average was about 11% (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:16]). The motivating context was spoken twice with different figures: "almost $770 million" in injury costs in the top five European leagues, 30% more than the prior season, in the introduction (K5a7C4b1Cwc [01:01]), and "nearly $800 million" last season in the results (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:46]); the captions do not reconcile the two. Other context figures in the introduction: a 71% increase in injury severity after the winter World Cup and a 15% increase in the first three months of the Premier League season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [01:01]). The conclusion repeats "approximately 13% fewer injuries" and "an 11% financial reduction in injury-related costs" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:18]).

**Why it works** — The figure is arithmetic on the model's own simulated injuries: fewer predicted injuries to high-wage players means fewer wages tied to unavailable players. The speakers give no further mechanism. Inference: the percentage depends on how the saved injuries are distributed across salary levels, which the talk does not show.

**When to apply** — As an example of expressing injury burden in the currency a club decision-maker uses. Inference: for a Baylor audience, the equivalent would be availability (games or practices missed by starters), not wages. Eric's baseline: coach-facing reports are built mostly by strength staff, with sport science staff providing reports where applicable (interview 2026-09-28, Q28, Explicit); no wage-based injury metric is in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a measured saving: it comes from simulations with an imputed workload and no club data, and the $770 million and $800 million figures conflict inside the talk (K5a7C4b1Cwc [01:01], [12:46]). Professional soccer wages do not map to college athletics, where the cost is competitive and academic availability, not salary. Single presenter with a startup interest.

**Example** — The speakers' own: Brighton, 22% lower salary cost tied to predicted injuries, versus an 11% average across clubs (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:16]).

**Related** — [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]]; [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]].

# About Half a Billion Dollars of MLB Salary Went to UCL Rehab, 2004 to 2014

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally reports a league-wide study, "under review" at the time of the talk, using public MLB data (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Window:** 2004 to 2014, chosen so that players who had surgery in 2014 had time to return (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Counts:** about 200 surgeries, and on average 180 days of MLB-calendar time missed (z_6M5r7031A [12:14]). About half the players were starters and half relievers, with a small proportion of closers (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Total:** adjusted to 2017 levels, "half a billion dollars" of salary lost over the period to rehab alone (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Excluded:** medical, travel and rehab costs; downtime before the surgery; lost team wins; trade value; and every minor league player (z_6M5r7031A [12:44] to [13:44]). He speculates the full cost might be 1 billion or 1.5 billion and says "I don't know" (z_6M5r7031A [13:44]).
- **Per player:** medical cost of about $50,000, which he calls conservative (z_6M5r7031A [11:13]).
- **Salary per WAR:** it "balloons" after surgery and does not return to the pre-surgery level until 3 years after the pitcher returns (z_6M5r7031A [10:43]). In Q&A he calls the salary-over-WAR calculation "relatively back of the envelope" and not adjusted (z_6M5r7031A [28:27]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism; this is an accounting of public salary data. Inference: it counts only direct salary during rehab, which is why the number is a floor on the speaker's own account.

**When to apply** — As an example of costing an injury type from public records by counting time missed and attaching a value. Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: a Baylor version would count games and practices missed by injury type and position group with Athletic Medicine, with no salary figure.

**When NOT to apply** — The study was under review, not published, at the time. Baylor athletes have no player salaries, so dollar figures and dollars per WAR do not transfer to college. The salary-per-WAR calculation is unadjusted and the speaker's own words are "back of the envelope." The 180-day figure is MLB calendar time. It is professional baseball pitchers only, and it counts surgeries, not all injuries.

**Example** — The speaker's own: about 200 surgeries over 2004 to 2014 and 180 MLB-calendar days missed on average, summing to half a billion 2017 dollars (z_6M5r7031A [12:14] to [12:44]).

# Passer-shooter pairs choose better shots the more catch-and-shoot attempts they share

**What it is** — Ben Alamar and Dean Oliver report that NBA passer-shooter pairs improve their shot selection as the pair accumulates catch-and-shoot attempts together. Taking a pair's value at 0% and following its first 200 catch-and-shoot attempts, the curve rises steeply: about 7% better shot selection in the first 50 attempts, then about another 4% up to 200 (o4rMbhsdk0I [09:43]). Players rarely get more than 200 such attempts in one season (o4rMbhsdk0I [09:43]). The pair does not reset to zero in the next season: the speaker says it starts "about five percent above where they started from", below the end of the prior season, and by the end of season two it is better than at the end of season one (o4rMbhsdk0I [10:14]). The units of the 7% and 4% are not defined in the captions (the measure is expected points per shot from their shot-quality model, so these are most likely relative changes in expected points; Inference).

**Why it works** — The speakers show three measurable drivers of the better shots: shorter two-point attempts, lower pressure on the passer, and more open shots, with about a 4% decline in pressure score over the first 100 shots (o4rMbhsdk0I [10:47], [11:18], [11:48]). They read this as the passer finding the partner sooner, before the defense reacts (o4rMbhsdk0I [11:48]). They do not test why the pair learns; the mechanism of learning itself is not given.

**When to apply** — As a prior for how fast a newly formed pairing should improve: steep early, then slower, with partial carry-over across seasons. Inference: for a new football pairing (transfer quarterback with new receivers), treat the first weeks of numbers as the steep part of a curve rather than as the pair's level. Eric's baseline: new movement patterns are expected to take roughly 3 to 4 weeks of practice to become efficient (course team position, speaker unconfirmed, Inferred). The talk agrees in direction but measures attempts, not weeks, so the time scales are not comparable.

**When NOT to apply** — The data are NBA catch-and-shoot attempts only: 1600 passer-shooter combinations with 10 to 50 attempts, averaging 1.12 points per attempt, 2023-24 season (o4rMbhsdk0I [07:38]). The speakers call the numbers rule of thumb (o4rMbhsdk0I [17:27]), say the results are statistically significant but noisy (o4rMbhsdk0I [21:03]), and say pair-level results are noisy and biased because one person typically did most of the passing to a shooter (o4rMbhsdk0I [21:33]). The effect is stronger for catch-and-shoot than for all shot types (o4rMbhsdk0I [24:07]). No age, rookie or role adjustments were made (o4rMbhsdk0I [35:23]). Football pass plays per quarterback-receiver pair are far fewer than repeated catch-and-shoot attempts (Inference). Do not use the curve to grade or rank individual pairs.

**Example** — The speakers' own example is the 2020-21 Phoenix Suns (see [[case-study--phoenix-suns-chris-paul-familiarity-ramp]]).

**Related** — [[framework--familiarity-counter-log-log-shot-quality-model]] (how the curve was built), [[claim--familiarity-gain-splits-between-shot-selection-and-accuracy]], [[claim--familiarity-gains-diminish-across-seasons]].

# Classify Chronotype, Then Time Peak Performance Relative to When the Athlete Wakes

**What it is** — A method the speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) describes from a study she attributes to a "university of Birmingham" (caption spelling) group. Competition-level athletes completed a paper-and-pencil morning-evening questionnaire, which classified them as early, intermediate or late (night owl) (J7smyg1Czik [17:22], [17:52]). Performance tests were done six times across the day: the bleep test (endurance, oxygen uptake) and sprint times, along with athletes' own ratings (J7smyg1Czik [17:52], [18:24]). As a whole group, performance was lowest at 7 am and highest in the late afternoon; the captions read "between four and seven" without am or pm (J7smyg1Czik [18:24], [18:55]). By chronotype, early types peaked between noon and 2, intermediate types in the mid-afternoon, and late types between 7 and 8 in the evening (J7smyg1Czik [18:55]). Relative to waking, early and intermediate types peaked about 6 to 7 hours after waking, and late types 11 hours or more after (J7smyg1Czik [19:58], [20:30]). A further analysis of a large number of athletes in 12 teams predicted team peak by team makeup: a team of mostly late types (T3) peaked later than a team of mostly early types (T10) (J7smyg1Czik [20:30], [21:00]). In the Q&A she says the body clock shifts mostly with light and can be moved with light boxes and melatonin, for example earlier bedtimes for a team trip to London, and that this takes discipline (J7smyg1Czik [29:02]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that a biological clock decides whether someone is a night owl or morning lark, and everyone's peak therefore differs (J7smyg1Czik [16:51], [17:22]). Her point is that a fixed wake time, imposed by a coach or schedule, does not shift when an individual peaks (J7smyg1Czik [19:58], [20:30]). She gives no mechanism for the questionnaire's validity.

**When to apply** — When choosing the time of day for testing or high-stakes sessions, or when comparing an athlete's results across times. Inference: record each athlete's test time and, if the staff wishes, the questionnaire result, before comparing sessions; this matters for repeatable testing. Eric's baseline (course material, speaker unconfirmed, tagged Inferred): testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April"). Eric's baseline: Eric has no stated chronotype practice; the baseline is silent.

**When NOT to apply** — Sample sizes are not stated for the questionnaire study; the only count is 12 teams. The study is competition-level athletes, not college football, and early-morning football practice and meal schedules are not under athletes' control. The speaker says the whole circadian advantage is "unexplored" (J7smyg1Czik [23:03]). Her claim that a third of teams she talks to are not interested is her own experience (J7smyg1Czik [28:31]). A light and melatonin protocol was mentioned, not described; do not use it as a medical recommendation.

**Example** — The speaker's own: Team 3, mostly late types, versus Team 10, mostly early types; she says if a morning game pitted them against each other, T3 would be at a biological disadvantage, and in the evening T10 would be (J7smyg1Czik [21:00], [21:32]).

15:Ben Alamar and Dean Oliver study whether NBA teammates shoot better the more they play together. They build a shot-quality model from NBA tracking and pressure data, then regress shot quality and accuracy on counters of how many catch-and-shoot attempts a passer and shooter have had together. They report a steep early gain over the first 50 attempts, slower gain to about 200, partial carry-over into the next season, and roughly half the gain from better shot selection and half from accuracy. The speakers call the numbers rule of thumb and stress noise. Most of the talk is a long audience Q&A raising possible extensions.

=================== framework--injury-coding-and-censoring-rules-for-load-analysis.md
---
kind: framework
chapter: "TbYgc6_qQzo"
topic: injury coding and censoring
category: [method, injury, training-load, data-quality]
confidence: supported
source: "TbYgc6_qQzo, SSAC18, Volume and Intensity in Injury Incidence in Football Athletes"
---

# How the Study Coded Injuries, Scaled Load and Censored Sessions

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") describes how his one-season football study handled the limitations he lists in other papers (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:41]):
1. **Injury definition:** any injury not due to contact with another player that results in the player missing subsequent training sessions or games, "really stringent" so only non-contact time-loss injuries counted (TbYgc6_qQzo [11:14] to [11:45]).
2. **Who coded:** a medical professional present at the diagnoses coded the injuries in a bespoke injury database (TbYgc6_qQzo [11:45]).
3. **Load scaling:** load variables normalized to session minutes (the density of the session), then standardized within each position group, to "borrow some strength" from position-group data because groups have different tasks (TbYgc6_qQzo [11:45] to [12:15]).
4. **Censoring:** an athlete who was injured in a session, evaluated by a medical professional and deemed unable to continue was removed from the data for that injury day, so the shortened session would not pull the data down (TbYgc6_qQzo [12:15] to [12:47]).
5. **Models:** logistic regression models, fit iteratively, with the caption reading "for" (likely "four") separate models for the load-variable groups plus a joint model; the model count is ambiguous in the caption (TbYgc6_qQzo [12:47]). Compared with the Bayesian information criterion and out-of-sample likelihood (TbYgc6_qQzo [12:47] to [13:18]).
6. **Out-of-sample check:** with too little data for a hold-out group, they used "a concept like leave one out cross validation" across the season (TbYgc6_qQzo [13:18]).

**Why it works** — Step 4 answers the problem he names earlier, that without censoring a model can show low loads leading to injuries (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:36]). Step 1 and 2 answer the contact and severity problem (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33] to [04:04]). The speaker gives no reason for position standardization beyond borrowing strength and position-specific tasks (TbYgc6_qQzo [12:15]).

**When to apply** — As a template for agreeing, between Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance, one injury definition and one rule for sessions where an athlete is injured, before any load analysis. Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Explicit, SportSmith article 2026-02-20, NordBord). Inference: consistent injury coding is the same kind of precondition. Eric's baseline: no sport- or position-specific GPS thresholds exist formally (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q7). Inference: the speaker's within-position standardization is one way to get position-specific load measures without published thresholds, though he gives no thresholds himself.

**When NOT to apply** — The out-of-sample check is leave-one-out style within one team's one season, which is not an independent test; the speaker calls it "a concept like" that method. Band thresholds for effort bands and IMA are fixed but their values are not given (TbYgc6_qQzo [08:42] to [09:12]). Position standardization did not produce a position effect with 29 injuries (TbYgc6_qQzo [15:22]). The talk reports no inter-rater check on the injury coding.

**Example** — The speaker's own scenario: an athlete injured and removed early in a session (his example is about a quarter of the way in) should be censored, not kept in the data with a tiny load (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:36]). His rule for his own study is step 4 above (TbYgc6_qQzo [12:15] to [12:47]).

**Related** — [[framework--checklist-for-reading-load-and-injury-papers]]. [[case-study--101-football-athletes-one-season-load-and-non-contact-injury]].
=================== framework--proper-mechanics-as-reference-range-of-healthy-fast-pitchers.md
---
kind: framework
chapter: "AgouMNTeyo4"
topic: reference range for mechanics
category: [biomechanics, reference-ranges, baseball]
confidence: supported
source: "AgouMNTeyo4, SSAC15, SSAC15: Analytics of the Tommy John Injury Epidemic with Glenn Fleisig"
---

# Defining "proper mechanics" as the mean and spread of healthy, high-velocity pitchers

**What it is** — Asked how he knows what proper mechanics are, Glenn Fleisig describes his criteria: the pitcher came to his lab, had not been injured for at least a year, and had a high fastball velocity during the test (AgouMNTeyo4 [54:32], [55:03]). He took about 150 such pitchers (by his account including Roger Clemens, and "some college guy you never heard of"), computed the mean and standard deviation of each measurement (stride length is his example), and calls that range proper mechanics: in effect the 150 best pitchers he has tested by ball velocity (AgouMNTeyo4 [55:03], [55:33]; the caption says "pictures", read here as pitchers). Studies then showed pitchers outside those ranges, as a group, had lower ball velocity and higher stress on the arm (AgouMNTeyo4 [55:33], [56:03]). He has also tested over 2,000 pitchers in the lab, including eight who went on to win Cy Young awards (caption "sa young", "15 sa young Awards"), with 12 cameras and about 40 markers (AgouMNTeyo4 [13:20], [13:51], [43:13]).

His own account of the limits: when asked whether pitchers measured with poor mechanics later got hurt, "it was a mixed bag", about half did and half did not. He says mechanics is only one factor, that his lab intervenes by telling pitchers what they do wrong (so some may fix it), and that the step from higher arm stress to more injury is "a leap of faith" that he has not proven (AgouMNTeyo4 [58:06], [58:38]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's logic is that good mechanics give more velocity and less arm stress, and bad mechanics more stress (AgouMNTeyo4 [24:45]). Inference: the benchmark is built from a selected, healthy, fast group, so a measure outside the range is a flag for a closer look, not a finding of risk.

**When to apply** — Building a reference range for any lab or field metric: define the reference group by outcome criteria (healthy for a stated time, high performance on a stated test), report the mean and standard deviation of each variable, and test whether being outside the range predicts the thing you care about.

Eric's baseline: force plate and monitoring thresholds are individualized, not fixed positional cut-offs: "Wednesdays, the thresholds should be individualized," against percent change from baseline or a rolling average, with standard deviations and the smallest worthwhile change used "to diagnose signal versus noise" (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a). Metrics are chosen by the output, driver, strategy and optional symmetry framework from Hawkin Dynamics (adopted practice, framework not Eric's own). Inference: Fleisig's group reference range is a between-athlete benchmark, where Eric's thresholds compare an athlete to his own baseline, so the two answer different questions. No sport- or position-specific thresholds exist formally at Baylor (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q7).

**When NOT to apply** — The benchmark is partly circular: "proper" is defined by high velocity and health, then the finding that people outside the range throw slower is close to built in. The follow-up on injury was mixed and unproven by his own account. The lab is baseball pitching. Do not use an out-of-range value to restrict an athlete by itself. The group's size (about 150) is stated, the criteria for "high velocity" are not, and results for the unpublished spring-training work are separate. Fleisig advises a motion-capture device company (AgouMNTeyo4 [41:13]); the devices in the talk were not validated in it.

**Example** — The speaker's own: stride length, where one pitcher's value is one number and another's another, and the group mean and standard deviation define the proper range (AgouMNTeyo4 [55:33]).

**Related** — [[claim--curveballs-not-shown-more-stressful-than-fastballs]]; [[case-study--spring-training-field-lab-post-surgery-vs-never-injured]] (field use of the same lab); [[principle--throwing-harder-raises-risk-and-performance]].
=================== heuristic--define-chemistry-narrowly-before-measuring-it.md
---
kind: heuristic
chapter: "o4rMbhsdk0I"
topic: define chemistry before measuring
category: [method, definitions, learning-curve, interventions]
confidence: untested
source: "o4rMbhsdk0I, SSAC25, Lessons in Chemistry: Impact of Teammate Familiarity on Shooting in the NBA"
---

# Define the slice of "chemistry" you measure, and set the normal curve before testing an intervention

**What it is** — Two method rules the speakers state in the Q&A. First, "anytime you try and study something like chemistry you have to define it": here chemistry means familiarity in catch-and-shoot situations only, "a very small subset of what chemistry could be" (o4rMbhsdk0I [30:45], [31:16]). Extending to lineup-level playing time and efficiency needs care because good lineups tend to play more together (o4rMbhsdk0I [31:16]). One speaker also names skill fit between two players as another meaning of chemistry, with a paddle-ball example where the more athletic player was less consistent than a partner who grew up playing it (o4rMbhsdk0I [31:46], [32:18], [32:48]); this is a personal anecdote. Second, to study learning or an intervention, "you have to have the starting point, what is the normal expected curve", and then see whether the intervention makes the curve better (o4rMbhsdk0I [30:15]).

**Why it works** — The speakers do not give a mechanism. Inference: a narrow definition keeps the measurement attributable to one thing, and a baseline curve prevents crediting an intervention for improvement that would have happened anyway. The talk's own result (steep early gain from repetition alone) shows the size of that default improvement.

**When to apply** — Before crediting a practice, testing or training change with a pair's or unit's improvement, establish how a comparable group's results normally move over the same number of reps or weeks. Eric's baseline: testing protocols must be exactly repeatable over time (course team position, speaker unconfirmed, Inferred), which is what makes a normal curve comparable. Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place" (interview 2026-09-28, Q3), which is the same test applied to a metric: name the question first.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the speakers' stated approach, not a validated procedure, so confidence is untested. The speakers also say that slicing curves by player, pair or location "potentially leads in to more insight but it also leads to more noise" (o4rMbhsdk0I [25:38]), so a narrow definition costs sample size. A normal curve needs a large comparison set; a small team or one position group may not supply it (Inference).

**Example** — The speaker's own: practice data held by teams could show whether small-sided practice shortens the curve, which is the prescriptive side; the NBA game data used in the talk cannot show it (o4rMbhsdk0I [20:32], [21:03]).

**Related** — [[framework--familiarity-counter-log-log-shot-quality-model]], [[claim--teammate-familiarity-improves-catch-and-shoot-shot-quality]].
=================== heuristic--strategic-nap-lengths-and-when-not-to-nap.md
---
kind: heuristic
chapter: "J7smyg1Czik"
topic: strategic napping
category: [sleep, naps, recovery, travel]
confidence: untested
source: "J7smyg1Czik, SSAC17, The Science of Sleep"
---

# Strategic Naps: 15 to 20 Minutes, 30 Minutes or 90 Minutes, and Not When Night Sleep Is Poor

**What it is** — In the Q&A, the speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) says nine hours in bed means nine hours over a 24-hour period, so an athlete who cannot sleep it all at once can nap (J7smyg1Czik [29:33]). She names three nap types: 15 to 20 minutes, after which you wake from light sleep and should feel refreshed; 30 minutes, which still ends in light sleep (stage two, she says); and a 90-minute "granddaddy" nap that goes through light, deep and dream sleep, after which you wake spontaneously (J7smyg1Czik [29:33], [30:03]). Her caution: if the athlete has trouble sleeping at night, a nap is "not a good thing," because it uses up the homeostatic sleep drive (J7smyg1Czik [30:35]). She also says trouble falling asleep in athletes usually comes from trying to sleep at an unusual time after crossing time zones (the example is four) or from heavy caffeine in the evening because games are in the evening (J7smyg1Czik [30:35]). She adds that napping after training helps, since sleep consolidates learning and memory formed in training (J7smyg1Czik [25:25]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism for the length choice is the sleep stage you wake from: light sleep in the short naps, a full cycle in the 90-minute nap. Her caution rests on sleep drive (time awake) opposing sleep, as she describes it earlier in the talk (J7smyg1Czik [11:45], [12:48]). No study is cited for the nap lengths.

**When to apply** — When an athlete's schedule leaves time in bed short, and nighttime sleep is otherwise good. Inference: the three lengths give a short and a long option for a travel day or a long gap between sessions. Eric's baseline: no sleep or nap protocol is in the baseline; recovery is managed through training-load design alone (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit).

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the nap guidance is the speaker's practical advice with no data, population or study cited. Not for athletes with poor night sleep (her own rule). The talk does not address timing relative to training or competition. Inference: a long nap close to a session may leave an athlete groggy, but the speaker does not say so. Not a substitute for a clinical sleep evaluation. Naps are a make-up for total sleep, not a replacement for regular nights, since she says deficits are cumulative (J7smyg1Czik [22:33]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: nine hours in bed counted over 24 hours, so a nap can make up time that one night did not (J7smyg1Czik [29:33]). Inference: a 15 to 20 minute nap fits a short gap between sessions; the 90-minute nap needs time to wake fully.

**Related** — [[heuristic--weekend-sleep-extension-signals-a-deficit]]; [[claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/lever-2024-a-preliminary-investigation-of-the-relationship-between-sleep-and-nap-behavior-of-ncaa-div]] (NCAA Division I nap behavior).
=================== principle--player-credit-is-a-causal-question-not-a-prediction-residual.md
---
kind: principle
chapter: "pcp9h_M6Ir8"
topic: causal versus residual credit
category: [football, causal-inference, player-evaluation, offensive-line]
confidence: contested
source: "pcp9h_M6Ir8, SSAC25, Causal Impact of Offensive Linemen on Pass Plays"
---

# Player Credit Is a Causal Question, Not a Prediction Residual

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins (senior data scientist at Sumer Sports, PhD student at Florida Atlantic University, pcp9h_M6Ir8 [00:00]) argues that "estimating player performance is fundamentally a causal problem yet it's often treated as a prediction problem" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [00:30]). The usual approach trains a model to predict an expected outcome (a conditional mean) and attributes the residual, actual minus predicted, to the player. His example is rush yards over expected: a back "expected to gain four yards" runs 26, and the 22-yard residual is credited to him (caption name "Damen Harris", pcp9h_M6Ir8 [02:00], [02:31]). Such metrics "solely rely on correlation based techniques" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [01:00]). He contrasts the two: machine learning predicts what is likely and "excels at pattern recognition", while causal inference "seeks to answer why and how something happens" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [02:31]). He claims, "based on our knowledge", this is the first public application of causal inference to the offensive line and one of few on NFL tracking data (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [00:00]).

**Why it works** — His stated reason is that a residual cannot say what would have happened under a different action by the player; the causal framing asks for the effect of the action on the outcome (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [01:00], [02:31]). The way he does it is in [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]].

**When to apply** — When a metric credits one player for an outcome that several teammates and opponents shaped (blocking, pressure, assist chains). Ask what the number conditions on, and whether it is a residual from a prediction model. Inference: this is a question to ask of vendor grades, and it applies to a residual such as the one in [[heuristic--credit-yards-above-expected-to-the-passer-with-selection-bias-caveat]].

Eric's baseline: "I think it's raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q12, about ACWR.) Inference: the same habit of asking what a single number leaves out is what this talk argues for; Eric's baseline has no causal-inference method of its own.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked contested. The talk is a method presentation by its builder (Sumer Sports), and its causal reading depends on assumptions the talk checks only partly (see [[framework--causal-model-robustness-checks-balance-placebo-sensitivity]]). The DeepQB talk (EeBgUCYhezc [12:23]) and the many residual metrics the speaker names treat the residual as credit; this talk disagrees with that approach, and the library does not hold evidence that settles it. Inference: residual metrics and causal estimates answer different questions (how a player compares with typical, versus what his action did), and both can be useful for a screening or scouting decision, so the principle should not be read as "residuals are wrong". The talk also says residual metrics "are useful" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [09:05]). Validation shown is against honors, salary and PFF, which agree with consensus and are not themselves a test of cause (see [[claim--clip-validation-against-honors-salary-and-pff]]).

**Example** — The speaker's: rush yards over expected on the handoff play, 4 expected and 26 gained, 22 attributed (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [02:00]).

**Related** — [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]]; [[heuristic--credit-yards-above-expected-to-the-passer-with-selection-bias-caveat]] (a residual method, contested by this principle); [[principle--credit-pass-rush-pressure-throughout-the-play]] (per-player credit by a descriptive model). Vault paper on a related rating approach: [[pipping-gamon-2026-opponent-adjusted-evaluation-of-nfl-pass-blocking-and-pass-rushing-performance]].

== claim--familiarity-gains-diminish-across-seasons.md
**What it is** — Asked about diminishing returns, a speaker answers that a third season would start lower than the peak at the end of season two but "not that different from the start of the second season", so marginal gains keep declining season to season (o4rMbhsdk0I [19:31]). The data set does not hold enough pairs who played together for long to find a theoretical maximum, but "two, three seasons together is beneficial" (o4rMbhsdk0I [20:01]).
